title: The Missing Alibi Again
premise: Estate lawyer Freya Villalobos is hired by a nervous stranger who pays in advance to prove that a murder in the town of Alderbrook hasn't happened yet — a murder dated three days from now, described in a will that names a witness everyone insists died years ago. As Freya traces the will's impossible provenance, she discovers her own firm's files have been quietly doctored for years, and the town's most powerful family has been laundering its sins through probate. The 'dead' witness, Marisol, is alive and hiding, holding testimony about a death the Vane family buried. In the end Freya must choose between protecting the client who hired her — who turns out to be the intended victim's estranged son — and exposing the truth: she files the will publicly, the murder is attempted but fails, and Alderbrook's alphabetized secrets finally spill into the open.
about_author: M. M. Oyelaran is the pen name of a former paralegal who spent a decade watching small-town secrets pass through probate court. They write mysteries where paperwork is as dangerous as any weapon.

chapters.title: Paid in Advance
chapters.summary: Freya Villalobos, third-person POV, takes on an unusual client: Elias Thorne, who pays double to hire her to prevent a murder scheduled for Friday — one he can describe in detail. The emotional beat is uneasy curiosity; Freya's instinct says walk away, but the retainer clears and her curiosity doesn't.

chapters.title: The Will That Wasn't Filed
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. She discovers a will in her own archive naming a beneficiary who supposedly died in 2019 — Marisol Quintero, key witness to the death of councilman Daniel Vane. The document's filing stamp is forged, and the forgery is good. Beat: professional dread; someone inside the system did this.

chapters.title: Alderbrook Remembers Nothing
chapters.summary: Third-person, alternating between Freya interviewing townsfolk and Elias watching the Vane estate. Everyone repeats the same polished story of Daniel Vane's accidental drowning. The uniformity itself becomes evidence. Beat: creeping isolation — the whole town is either lying or memory-wiped by loyalty.

chapters.title: The Widow's Perfect Grief
chapters.summary: Freya meets Camille Vane, the widow, now matriarch of the family law practice that once employed Freya's mentor. Camille is gracious, generous, and asks one question too precisely: what exactly brought you back to the 2019 file? Beat: charm as a weapon; power smiling.

chapters.title: Three Days to Friday
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. He explains how he knows the murder details — he received letters, dated in advance, describing each event before it happened. The latest letter describes Friday night at the boathouse. Beat: mounting panic; time made physical, a countdown Freya pins above her desk.

chapters.title: Files, Alphabetized
chapters.summary: Freya audits her firm's records overnight and finds eleven files altered over three years — all touching the Vane name, all bearing her own login stamps. Someone has been framing her paper trail for years. Beat: betrayal and paranoia; her ordered world turned against her.

chapters.title: The Grave Without a Body
chapters.summary: Freya and Elias visit Marisol Quintero's grave and find the plot empty beneath the marker — a purchased headstone, no interment record. Beat: grim exhilaration; the first hard proof that the town's official memory is manufactured.

chapters.title: What the Mentor Knew
chapters.summary: Flashback-heavy chapter, Freya's POV, visiting her retired mentor Ruth Okafor, who drafted the original 2019 will and has since gone silent. Ruth gives her a sealed envelope and one warning: don't open it until you're ready to lose something. Beat: loyalty tested against truth.

chapters.title: The Boathouse at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Third-person surveillance chapter. Freya stakes out the boathouse two nights early and finds fresh rope, a cleaned patch of floor, and a hidden camera still recording. Someone is preparing the stage. Beat: cold fear sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Marisol, Alive
chapters.summary: Following the camera's feed, Freya finds Marisol Quintero living under another name two counties over. Marisol saw Daniel Vane die — murdered by his brother Adrian — and ran when the sheriff's report called her a liar. Beat: relief curdling into terror; the witness everyone swears is dead wants to stay dead.

chapters.title: Testimony Refused
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She refuses to testify: last time, her sister lost her job, her landlord evicted her, and a car followed her for months. Freya must convince her without promising safety she can't guarantee. Beat: the cost of truth made concrete and human.

chapters.title: The Son Who Hired Her
chapters.summary: Freya confronts Elias with what she's learned and he confesses: he is Adrian Vane's estranged son, and the letters predicted his father would kill again — this time targeting Ruth Okafor. Beat: shattered trust; the client was a son trying to stop his own blood.

chapters.title: Thursday's Small Murders
chapters.summary: Interlocking third-person vignettes: Ruth's brakes fail, Marisol's safehouse address leaks, and Freya's bar complaint is filed anonymously. None are fatal; all are messages. Beat: pressure tightening like a vise; corruption working through ordinary channels.

chapters.title: Camille's Ledger
chapters.summary: Freya breaks into the Vane family office and finds Camille's private ledger — decades of payments, hush money, and filed favors, including entries matching every altered file in Freya's firm. Beat: horrified clarity; the widow has been the architect all along.

chapters.title: The Envelope
chapters.summary: Freya finally opens Ruth's envelope: the original, unaltered 2019 will plus Ruth's signed affidavit — and a note admitting Ruth altered the copies herself to protect Marisol, then lost her nerve. Beat: grief and forgiveness; even allies bend under power's weight.

chapters.title: Friday Morning
chapters.summary: Freya tries to go to the state police and finds the local sheriff already waiting — with a warrant for her arrest on evidence-tampering charges, timed perfectly. Beat: the trap closing; the system itself deployed as a weapon.

chapters.title: Out on Paper
chapters.summary: Freed on technicality by a young deputy who read the leaked ledger, Freya goes underground with Elias and Marisol. They plan to serve the will publicly at the Vane gala Friday night, forcing it into the record before the murder can be staged. Beat: desperate hope; paperwork as insurrection.

chapters.title: The Gala
chapters.summary: Third-person, high tension. At the Vane estate gala, Freya serves the will before two hundred witnesses while Adrian Vane watches from the mezzanine. Camille calmly announces the document is fraudulent. Beat: public defiance; the moment truth stops being deniable.

chapters.title: Boathouse, Friday Night
chapters.summary: Adrian, exposed, moves up his plan: lure Marisol to the boathouse using a text from Elias's stolen phone. Freya realizes the trap mid-gala and races ahead of the sheriff. Beat: breathless pursuit; the predicted murder arriving on schedule.

chapters.title: The Witness Speaks
chapters.summary: Climax. At the boathouse, Adrian corners Marisol; Freya arrives and stalls him with the one thing he fears — a live-streamed deposition already running, deputy Reyes listening. Adrian confesses in rage; deputies take him down. Beat: catharsis; the dead witness testifies at last.

chapters.title: Probate of a Dynasty
chapters.summary: Aftermath, Freya's POV. Adrian is charged; Camille, untouchable on paper, dismantles her empire and vanishes, leaving the ledger to the state. Ruth's affidavit stands. Freya refiles every altered record by hand. Beat: weary justice; some accounts close, some only transfer.

chapters.title: Filed Under Q
chapters.summary: Epilogue. Months later, Freya opens a new drawer in her cabinet labeled QUINTERO and finds a thank-you letter from Marisol, now testifying before a grand jury — and a fresh envelope, postmarked Alderbrook, containing a new will that shouldn't exist. Beat: quiet dread and wry resolve; the archivist's work is never done.
